outputs.notable: Substantive error in finding 7: "A due date of `2026-09-19` can reach the client as `2026-09-18T04:00:00.000Z` — the wrong calendar day." The direction is wrong for the offset implied. node-postgres parses a `date` to local midnight; at UTC-4 that serializes as `2026-09-19T04:00:00.000Z`, which still carries the right calendar date. The wrong-day failure occurs at positive UTC offsets (e.g. UTC+2 gives `2026-09-18T22:00:00.000Z`). The underlying concern is real, the worked example is not. Also: the "Tests that would have caught each defect" table numbers two consecutive rows "6". Its corrected handler uses pg-promise named parameters (`$(id)`) while the artifact used positional `$1` — valid, but an unflagged convention change. On substance it is otherwise strong, and it is the only output to raise `due_date` serialization and unfiltered `status` at all.

methodology_notes:
Three calls could reasonably have gone the other way, and one of them decides two scores.

1. Item 1 (tri-state verdict) on W and Z. Both emit the single token "NOT VERIFIED" and neither prints the full scale or names an intermediate state. I credited them because "NOT VERIFIED" is recognizably one value of the tri-state vocabulary the checklist itself names, and because W treats it as a scale value ("the verdict, which is already NOT VERIFIED on D1 and D2 alone"). A stricter judge could hold that emitting one label does not demonstrate a three-way scheme, and would then mark item 1 absent for all four outputs. Nothing in X or Y is close either way — both give prose conclusions ("fails the contract. Do not merge.") — so this only affects W and Z.

2. Item 4 (ranks defects by severity) on X. X's eight findings do descend in severity, and it argues comparative severity for the top two ("Defects 1 and 2 compound into the worst outcome available here. Neither alone is as bad as the pair"). But it carries no severity labels and never states that the order is a ranking, so crediting it requires me to infer the ordering from the content. Under the "a vague gesture in the right direction is absent" rule I marked it absent. Y, whose findings are equally unlabelled, got credit solely because it wrote the words "Findings, worst first" — that is a thin distinction between two otherwise similar structures, and I want it on the record that the difference is one heading.

3. Item 6 (receipt per clean axis) on X. Its "Parameterized SQL — correct, and genuinely so. `$1` with a value array" is an actual receipt. Its "Session required — correct as stated" is not. The item says "for each axis it calls clean", so one receipt out of three fails it, and partial credit does not exist. A judge reading item 6 as "does it ever give receipts" would credit X.

Two limits on the whole exercise. First, the artifact under review (handler, contract, schema, producer's note) is not in the bundle, so I could not verify any output's factual claims against the source. Everything in `notable` about substance rests on internal consistency, cross-output disagreement, and general knowledge of pg-promise / node-postgres / Node — not on the code. Y's "four clauses" vs. everyone else's three is the clearest case: I can report the disagreement but not resolve it. Second, items 1, 2, 3 and 5 partition the bundle identically (W and Z present, X and Y absent), which makes the four outputs look like two pairs. I scored each independently and re-read each for each item, but I cannot rule out that seeing the pattern after the first two items made the later calls feel more obvious than they were.
